en: *The Commentary on the Principles of the Prajñāpāramitā: The Sūtra of the Great Bliss Vajra Amoghasiddhi Samaya*, Volume One.
By the Grand Master of the Court, Peer of the State, Special Advancement, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, Tripitaka Master of Daixingshan Monastery, who was the Duke of Sū Kingdom with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously honored as Minister of Works, and bestowed the title Dajian (Great Mirror) and the epithet Dayangzhi (Great Extensive Wisdom), by imperial decree. Thus it is said.
This refers to the sūtra indicated at the time of the council.
The phrase "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) serves to signify that [the teaching] was heard directly from the Buddha.
"At one time" means that at the moment the sutra was being preached,
the earth shook in six ways.
Alternatively, the heavens may rain down various flowers—
a phenomenon that does not occur at other times.
Furthermore, those of the lineages of the three vehicles all attain the fruits of sainthood.
It is thus called "at one time. As for the term Bhagavat, it has the meaning of "one who can destroy.
That which is destroyed refers to the destruction of the four māras.
Furthermore, there are six meanings as explained in the *Śabdavidyā* (Treatise on Phonology):
brilliance, sovereignty, and magnificence, and so forth.
As for "accomplishing the sublime," it refers to this.
Vairocana is the self-awakened noble wisdom (*svasaṃvidāryajñāna*). "All Tathāgatas" refers,
according to the *Yogācāra* teachings, to the five Buddhas.
As for these five Buddhas,
they are the entirety of the Buddhas throughout the void of space and the pervasive Dharma-realm,
gathered without end or remainder to form these five bodies.
The Vajra-empowerment represents the Tathāgata’s ten suchnesses, ten dharma-realms, and ten tathāgata-stages; by means of these,
it forms the ten peaks above and below of the Great Space of Vajra Wisdom.
"Empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) signifies that from within the Middle Way, the wisdom of Samantabhadra and the sixteen great bodhisattvas flows forth in successive succession.
Together they constitute thirty-seven positions.
Thus is completed the Great Maṇḍala of the Wheel of Liberation for those possessing the wisdom of the samaya.
This is both a vow and a maṇḍala.
Do not allow those of the Supreme Vehicle in the future to receive [the teachings] solely on their own initiative without receiving them from a teacher.
Therefore, it is known that those who practice the Supreme Vehicle must receive the samaya from a master before they may engage in its cultivation.
Having already attained the precious crown of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas and become the sovereign of the three realms,
the Tathāgata, while still on the stage of the causal ground,
[received it] from the preceptor of empowerment.
Entering the Samaya-jñāna-maṇḍala,
the ācārya empowers the body of the disciple, wherein the tathāgatagarbha-nature originally exists,
and invokes vajra-empowerment.
By thus perfecting the practitioner as a vessel for the mantras and conduct of a bodhisattva,
one becomes fit for the stages of empowerment, such as those of the Vidyādhara and up to the transmission and authorization of consecration;
this serves as the primary cause.
Through the correspondence with the three secrets and the four wisdom seals,
one becomes the ultimate sovereign of the Dharma-kings of the triple world;
this constitutes the fruition.
He has already realized the sovereign mastery of the yoga of the omniscient wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
Regarding the phrase "having already realized all Tathāgatas," this refers to the five Buddhas mentioned above.
The wisdom of omniscience is the wisdom personally realized by the Buddha alone;
it is entirely in accord with the methods of yoga.
Having attained mastery over the Dharma, one is able to perform all the seals (*mudrā*) of all Tathāgatas; this is the Seal of the Four Wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-mudrā*).
It brings to complete fulfillment all various activities of equality and all intentions and deeds for the sake of the entire realm of sentient beings, without end or remainder.
They are capable of acting.
Because they have attained mastery over yoga, all Tathāgatas are able to act.
The five Buddhas are also explained as before.
Each Buddha possesses the wisdom of the equality of all seals and activities (*sarvamudrā-samatva-karmapada-jñāna*),
which reaches throughout all infinite and exhaustive Buddha-fields and realms of sentient beings.
They are able to perform various kinds of benefit,
ultimately bringing complete fulfillment to the entire realm of sentient beings—
whether superior, middling, or inferior.
Each and every one achieves the nine grades of *siddhi*.
Regarding "at all times throughout the three periods of eternity":
this refers to the body, speech, and mind activities of the Vajra Mahāvairocana Tathāgata. As for "eternity": [it means]...
This represents the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the pure dharma-realm,
which has been primordially present from beginningless time;
it remains undiminished even while dwelling amidst afflictions.
It is associated with pure dharmas;
it realizes purity without increase.
As for the "three periods of time":
This refers to the past, future, and present.
"At all times" means during the time of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Later, when the fruit of sainthood is realized,
the three karmas are pure like space;
this is because the actions of body, speech, and mind are not defiled by the afflictions born of false conceptualization.
"Vajra" refers to the attainment of mastery over all phenomena upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood,
and the realization of the three secrets of body, speech, and mind as vajra.
Within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
the habitual tendencies of afflictions cultivated through the path are as firm as a diamond, difficult to destroy.
By means of the samādhi of the Great Emptiness Vajra Wisdom, he realized the Dharmakāya, the Tathāgata Vairocana of Pervasive Radiance.

As the Sūtra says: "He dwells in the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven within the Desire Realm—a place where all Tathāgatas constantly roam—a majestic and praised Great Maṇi Hall adorned with various interspersed bells, silk banners, pearl necklaces, and ornaments such as half-moons and full moons, all shaken by a gentle breeze."
The palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is called the summit of the desire realm;
it is the celestial palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartins, where bodhisattvas reside.
Having realized the sixth stage,
the Bodhisattva of the Stage of Presence dwells in the contemplation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
He frequently served as a king among the hosts of these devas,
preaching the Prajñāpāramitā to gods and humans within that celestial realm.
The five desires are superior and transcend those of the devas;
therefore, Vairocana Buddha becomes Vajrasattva.
It explains great bliss and great passion;
it is the swift principle of yoga for manifest realization through empowerment.
By means of this, one hears that which is unstained by the various afflictions of worldly defilement.
Transcending the realm of Māra,
its palace is the Great Maṇḍala of the Mahāsukha-Amoghasiddhi-Vajrasattva.
All these arise from the store of merit of Vairocana Buddha.
This maṇḍala is a vajra-peak jewel-palace composed of the five great and wondrous vajra jewels.
It has four sides and eight pillars,
arranged in eight positions,
with four gates.
The central position is that of Vairocana, the All-Illuminating Tathāgata;
it is the liberation through the wisdom of internal realization.
These eight positions shall be explained later.

The Sūtra says: "Together with an assembly of eighty koṭis of bodhisattvas—namely, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajramuṣṭi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadyaścittotpādadharmacakrapravartin, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvamārapramardin—he taught the Dharma while surrounded by such a multitude of great bodhisattvas who paid him respectful homage."
Each of these bodhisattvas of the same class and lineage has a retinue of ten koṭis;
such is the case for the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
Within the moon disc before Vairocana,
it represents the bodhicitta of all Tathāgatas and the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment.
Through the empowerment of Vajrasattva,
one practices and realizes the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra,
and attains the stage of the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is situated upon the lunar disc behind Vairocana;
he represents the great compassion of all Tathāgatas.
Following conditions within the six realms of existence,
they rescue and deliver all sentient beings from the afflictions and sufferings of birth and death.
One swiftly realizes the pure samādhi,
neither clinging to saṃsāra nor realizing nirvāṇa;
all of this is through the direct realization of the Vajradharma of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
As for the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha,
he is situated upon the moon disc to the right of Vairocana;
he represents the accumulation of the merit and provisions of the Tathatā (Suchness) of all Tathāgatas, as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
By practicing the conduct of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha,
one practices four kinds [of giving],
which will be explained later.
The three spheres being pure, like space,
they are inexhaustible, conditioned, and untainted;
they constitute the provisions for the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi is on the moon disc to the left of Vairocana;
he represents the three kinds of secrets of all Tathāgatas.
In the palm of the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi,
by means of the mantra-practice of a bodhisattva who has entered the maṇḍala-cakra and received empowerment.
By hearing this secret teaching on the three karmas of the Tathāgata and practicing it,
one attains the supreme siddhis of both the mundane and supramundane realms,
and completely purifies the ten types of unwholesome and evil karma from beginningless time.
He has realized the ultimate wisdom that is free from all obstructions.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is situated within a moon disc in the southeast corner.
It represents the sword of wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā* of all Tathāgatas.
Abiding in the three gates of liberation, it is able to manifest the true nature of the *dharmakāya*: permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
By realizing this wisdom, the bodhisattva attains perfect enlightenment. This refers to the bodhisattva who,
upon the mere arousal of the thought of awakening, turns the wheel of Dharma.
In the southwestern corner is a moon disc,
representing the four kinds of wheels of all Tathāgatas: the Vajradhātu wheel, the Dharma wheel,
the Saṃbhoga wheel, and the Nirmita wheel.
The Cakravartin Trailokyavijaya,
the Cakravartin Sarvārthasiddhi,
and the Cakravartin Sarvaduṣṭavasa.
By practicing the conduct of mantra through the cultivation of true speech and action,
the bodhisattva enters such wheels as these, relying upon the four kinds of wisdom seals (jñānamudrā),
thereby accomplishing the arising of the sixteen great bodhisattvas.
He then realized unsurpassed bodhi.
As for the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
he resides in the northwest corner.
This is the ritual for the vast offerings to all Tathāgatas.
It is performed by a bodhisattva who, through the cultivation of the yoga of mantra and conduct, has attained the *yoga-samādhi* of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
In a single moment of thought,
their bodies were born before each and every Buddha throughout the entirety of space and the pervasive Dharma-realm,
amidst great assemblies.
They made offerings with various clouds and oceans,
presenting them to the Tathāgatas,
and then [departed] from all the Buddhas.
Hearing the exposition of the sublime Dharma,
they swiftly fulfill the provisions of merit and wisdom,
taking space as their treasury.
Following conditions across the various realms of existence,
they rescue and benefit all sentient beings,
gradually leading them toward unsurpassed bodhi.
Regarding this as skillful means,
the Bodhisattva Sarvamāradharṣaṇa is located in the northeast corner.
This manifests the great compassionate skillful means of all Tathāgatas:
externally manifesting majestic wrath while internally harboring compassion and pity.
Abiding in the stage of preparatory application,
one guards and sustains the practice,
eliminating all obstacles.
Upon attaining bodhi,
he shall subdue Māra, the devas, Maheśvara, and all those who are difficult to tame,
causing them to undergo transformation.
They attain unsurpassed bodhi and reach ultimate perfection through wrathful wisdom.
These are the eight great bodhisattvas as explained above.
It comprises three dharmas:
namely, the bodhicitta and great compassion.
This is skillful means (*upāya*).
As explained above, the various bodhisattvas encompass all the mantra gateways of the Buddha-dharma as well as all the manifest Mahāyāna.
Thus, this assembly of great bodhisattvas respectfully surrounds [the Buddha].
The eight offerings and the bodhisattvas of the four gates symbolize the retinue of the Tathāgata’s samādhi.
As for the scripture’s statement that "he teaches the Dharma, excellent in the beginning, middle,
and end," what is the Dharma being taught?
It is the *prajñāpāramitā-naya* (the principle of wisdom) of the great bodhisattvas.
"Good in the beginning" refers to the body-secrecy of all Tathāgatas,
which consists of all mudrās and bodily postures.
Regarding the excellence of the middle:
the secret speech of all Tathāgatas—
the instructions and commands of the Dharma King of mantras and dhāraṇīs— must not be transgressed.
The "excellent later" refers to the yoga of the *iṣṭadevatā*,
all *samādhis*, immeasurable wisdom, and liberation.
Another interpretation:
"good in the beginning" refers to the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*);
"good in the middle" refers to the training in higher mental cultivation (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).
The "excellent in the end" refers to the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
"Skillful in words and meaning" means skillful in words.
According to the science of phonology (*śabdavidyā*), his diction and rhythm were refined and elegant,
possessing all sixty-four varieties of Sanskrit resonance.
Regarding the "wondrous meaning," it relies upon the two truths:
the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.
"Pure and uniform" indicates that the Tathāgata’s yoga is not shared with the teachings of the three vehicles; therefore,
it refers solely to the Tathāgata’s ultimate, internally realized wisdom of the joy of the Dharma-garden, which is the uncommon Buddha-dharma.
As for "perfection":

by means of the aforementioned wisdom, one abandons all afflictions and their habitual tendencies throughout the nine stages of the three realms via both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,
thereby severing the two types of obscurations.
It is the perfection of the two kinds of provisions.
"Purified" indicates the purity of being free from defilement.
Through the method of yoga,
by bringing a single thought-moment of pure mind into correspondence [with reality],
one immediately realizes the suchness of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Without abandoning great compassion,
one attains Buddhahood through the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in both pure and impure lands.
The Sūtra states: "That which is pure white" refers to the dharmadhātu,
which is fundamentally unstained by immeasurable defilements.
The ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) that shrouds ordinary beings does not diminish in its nature,
even as they enter the stream of the noble ones and realize the stage of Buddhahood.
Its nature likewise does not increase.
As the Sūtra says, the "gate of the phrase of the purity of all phenomena" is for the sake of those who practice yoga.
Because they are unstained by the cycle of birth and death;
because they extensively perform deeds that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
and because they swiftly realize immeasurable samādhis, liberations, and wisdom.
Because they swiftly gather the vast provisions of merit,
they transcend all hosts of Māras and Vināyakas;
because they swiftly attain the fulfillment of supreme worldly and world-transcending aspirations.
It is said that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion,
takes pity upon those of the lineage of the Supreme Vehicle and liberates them through seventeen kinds of pure yoga-samādhis.
Therefore, the various sūtras state that the three realms are mind-only;
through the purification of the mind, sentient beings are purified.
Sentient beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind;
furthermore, it is said that the realm of sentient beings is the pure and sublime buddha-field of a bodhisattva,
which is realized through the cultivation of the seventeen gates of purification.
The Sūtra states: "That which is called the phrase of wondrous ease and purity is the stage of a Bodhisattva.
Regarding "wondrous ease," this is the Sanskrit term *sukha*.
*Sūrata* means that just as in the world there is the entertainment of *nara* and *nārī*,
so too is Vajrasattva *sūrata*.
With great compassion that is without objective referent,
one universally takes as object the inexhaustible realm of sentient beings,
vowing that they may attain peace, happiness, and benefit.
Because the mind never rests and because self and other are equal and non-dual,
it is called *sūrata*.
This arises from practicing the samādhi of the yoga of Vajrasattva.
One attains the phrase of wondrous, sublime, and pure realization;
therefore, one obtains the stage of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
That the phrase of the purity of the arrow of desire constitutes the stage of a bodhisattva—
By practicing the samādhi of the desire-vajra yoga,
one attains the purifying phrase of the desire-arrow;
therefore, one achieves the rank of the Bodhisattva Desire-Vajra.
Regarding the statement that "the phrase of the purity of touch is the stage of a bodhisattva":
by practicing the *vajra-śikhara-vigraha-yoga-samādhi*,
one attains the phrase of the purity of touch.
Therefore, one attains the bodhisattva stage of Vajramukuṭa-vigata-āpatti.
Regarding the statement that "the pure phrase of the bond of passion is the bodhisattva stage," this is because of practicing the samādhi of the Vajrayoga of the Bond of Passion.
One attains the phrase of the purity of the bond of craving;
therefore, one obtains the rank of the Bodhisattva Love-Vajra.
The phrase of the purity of the Sovereign Lord of All is the rank of the Bodhisattva.
By practicing the vajra-vaśitā-yoga samādhi,
one attains the pure syllable of all sovereign lords;
therefore, one obtains the rank of the Bodhisattva Vajravaśitā.
Regarding the statement that "seeing the pure state is the stage of a bodhisattva":
by practicing the vajra-yoga samādhi of the mind-born [body],
one attains the vision of the pure state.
Therefore, one attains the stage of the Vajra Bodhisattva of Mind-born [Nature].
Regarding the phrase "the stage of the Bodhisattva is the state of joy and purity":
this is because of practicing the samādhi of the yoga of the Vajra of Joy.
One attains the phrase of "pleasurable purity.
Therefore, one obtains the stage of the Bodhisattva Vajra-pleasure.
That the phrase of "purity of love" is the Bodhisattva stage—
By practicing the samādhi of the yoga of Rāgavajra,
one attains the syllable of the purity of desire;
therefore, one obtains the rank of the Bodhisattva Rāgavajra.
Regarding the statement that "the stage of a bodhisattva is the phrase of the purification of pride":
by practicing the vajra-pride yoga-samādhi,
one attains the phrase of the purification of pride.
Therefore, one attains the bodhisattva stage of Vajragarva.
Regarding the statement that "the stage of the Bodhisattva is the adornment of the pure syllable," this is due to practicing the Vajrayoga samādhi of Spring.
One attains the phrase of adorned purity;
therefore, one obtains the rank of the Bodhisattva Spring-Vajra.
That the phrase of the mind’s moistening purity is the rank of a Bodhisattva—
By practicing the samādhi of the Cloud-Vajra Yoga,
one attains the phrase of the moisture and purity of the mind,
also known as the phrase of the purity of joy.
Therefore, one attains the rank of the Bodhisattva Cloud-Vajra.
Regarding the statement that "the phrase of luminous purity is the rank of a Bodhisattva," this is due to practicing the samādhi of the Autumn Vajra Yoga.
One attains the phrase of luminous purity;
therefore, one obtains the stage of the Bodhisattva Autumn Vajra.
As for the phrase "the purity of bodily bliss," this is the stage of the Bodhisattva.
By practicing the samādhi of the Winter Vajra Yoga,
one attains the phrase of the purification of bodily bliss;
therefore, one obtains the rank of the Bodhisattva Winter Vajra.
Regarding the statement that "the phrase of the purity of form is the stage of a bodhisattva":
by practicing the samādhi of the vajra-yoga of form,
one attains the phrase of the purity of form.
Therefore, one attains the bodhisattva stage of Rūpavajra.
Regarding the phrase "the stage of the bodhisattva of the purity of sound":
by practicing the samādhi of the yoga of Śabdavajra, one attains the phrase of the purity of sound.
Therefore, one attains the bodhisattva stage of Ghoṣavajra.
Regarding the phrase "the purity of fragrance is the bodhisattva stage," this is because of practicing the samādhi of the fragrance-vajra yoga.
One attains the phrase of the purity of fragrance;
therefore, one obtains the rank of the Bodhisattva Gandhavajra.
As for the phrase of the purity of taste being the rank of a Bodhisattva:
By practicing the samādhi of the yoga of the flavor-vajra,
one attains the syllable of the purity of flavor;
therefore, one obtains the rank of the Bodhisattva Flavor-Vajra.
Why is it that the perfection of wisdom is pure because all phenomena are pure by nature? Although all phenomena are primordially pure, [the perfection of wisdom is so designated].
Due to the habitual tendencies of adventitious afflictions,
which veil the body and mind, one wanders through the six realms of cyclic existence.
By attaining the four seals of wisdom (*jñānamudrā*) according to the principles of yoga, [one transcends them].
That is to say: the Great Wisdom Seal,
the Samaya Wisdom Seal, and the Dharma Wisdom Seal.
Regarding the Karma-jñāna-mudrā:
as with each of the aforementioned Bodhisattvas, one must possess all four types of mudrās;
only when they are in correspondence can one attain stainless purity.
One immediately realizes the stage of the Great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra;
yet, even if one possesses the conditions, should the four wisdom-seals not be attained, it shall be as the sutras describe: "Hearing this but once with the ear."
One will obtain supreme merit that is certainly no different [from others],
and it shall serve as the direct cause for swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Vajrapāṇi, if anyone hears this Prajñāpāramitā-naya of the Birth of Purity,
then until they reach the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
all obscurations— namely, the afflictive obscurations, the cognitive obscurations, and the karmic obscurations— will be eliminated.
If one extensively accumulates [merit], one will certainly not fall into the realms of hell and so forth;
even if one has committed grave offenses, it is not difficult to extinguish them.
This is provided that one can receive and uphold [this teaching], reciting and chanting it daily, and reflecting upon it with focused attention.
In this very life, one realizes the vajra-samādhi of the equality of all phenomena;
one attains mastery over all phenomena and experiences immeasurable joy and delight.
Those who have attained the status of Tathāgata and Vajradhara through birth as sixteen great bodhisattvas—
Vairocana Buddha, amidst the great assembly,
for the sake of future sentient beings practicing yoga—
For the sake of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages,
it is taught that by upholding, reciting, and fully practicing [this teaching],
one will swiftly extinguish the immeasurable and heavy karmic obstructions accumulated since beginningless time.
Until the end of the future,
through the power of vast vows born of compassion,
they shall wander throughout the six realms of existence to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Through hearing and cultivation,
one does not become defiled by or subject to the ripening of unwholesome karma,
and attains mundane and supramundane supreme siddhis.
Immediately within the sixteen great births,
one becomes Vajrasattva Bodhisattva and so forth, up to Vajramuṣṭi Bodhisattva;
in the final body, one then attains the body of Vairocana.

At that time, the Bhagavān, the Supreme Sattva who holds the Vajra of all Maṇḍalas of the Mahāyāna-saṃdhi-mudrā of all Tathāgatas, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi—who has tamed all beings within the three realms without exception and is the Accomplisher of All Aims—desiring to clarify this meaning, smiled with a joyful countenance; he formed the Vajra-ābhimāna mudrā with his left hand, brandished the primordial Great Vajra with his right hand in a posture of heroic valor, and proclaimed Great Bliss.
Regarding the "Vajra-Asaṃvara-Samaya-Citta":
the meaning of *Bhagavat* is as explained previously.
As for "all Tathāgatas":
These are the five directional Buddhas within the Great Maṇḍala.
The Mahāyāna has seven meanings;
the first is the greatness of the Dharma.
Second is the greatness of mind;
third is the greatness of resolute belief;
fourth is the greatness of intention.
Fifth is the greatness of the provisions;
sixth is the greatness of time;
seventh is the greatness of the ultimate consummation.
It is by relying on this Great Vehicle that bodhisattvas realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
as for "actualizing," it means...
It is the object of samādhi realized by the yogācāras.
*Samaya* is termed the "original vow."
It is also called "time" (kāla) and "appointed agreement" (samaya).
It is also another name for the maṇḍala. As for all maṇḍalas:
Within the four types of maṇḍalas of this family:
first, the Great Maṇḍala; second, the Samaya Maṇḍala.
The Dharma Maṇḍala, and fourth, the Karma Maṇḍala.
By means of these four kinds of maṇḍalas.
The "Vajra Supreme Sattva" who encompasses all maṇḍalas of yoga refers to the vajra-meaning of bodhicitta.
"Victorious" (Jina) means most excellent;
"Sattva" signifies courage.
He is the one who disciplines [beings] within the three realms.
The three realms refer to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Within these,
he is able to subdue those among the gods who are difficult to tame, such as Maheśvara and others,
causing them all to receive transformation and instruction without exception.
Sarvārthasiddha is an alternative name for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is...
This Bodhisattva was originally Samantabhadra;
he personally received the five-wisdom vajra scepters from the two palms of Vairocana Buddha.
He immediately conferred upon him the empowerment and named him Vajrapāṇi,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
As previously explained,
"in order to further clarify this meaning" refers to elucidating the insignia of the seal of great wisdom (*mahājñānamudrā*).
On his head he wears a precious crown of the five Buddhas;
he smiles with a joyful countenance,
and his left hand forms the Vajragarva mudrā.
With his right hand, he draws forth and hurls the Primordial Great Vajra;
assuming a posture of heroic valor,
"primordial" refers to the originally pure *dharmadhātu*.
The left hand forms the Vajragarva mudrā in order to subdue sentient beings who follow heterodox paths and move to the left,
causing them to return to and conform to the true path; the right hand brandishes and hurls the five-wisdom vajra, assuming a posture of heroic valor.
May they cause themselves and others to enter the profound samādhi,
to advance step by step along the Buddha-way in every thought-moment,
and to attain the stage of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.

One attains stainless purity.
Regarding the *hṛdaya* (heart-essence) consisting of four syllables, which forms a single mantra as the gateway of the syllable *ha*:
it signifies that the cause of all phenomena is unattainable.
The syllable RA-gate is the meaning of all phenomena being free from dust.
"Dust" refers to the five sense objects;
it is also called the twofold attachment of grasper and grasped.
The gateway of the letter *i* signifies that sovereignty cannot be apprehended.
The meaning of the two dots is the letter *a*.
The letter *a* is named *nirvāṇa*.
Because one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn,
both types of attachment are abandoned,
and the purity of the dharmadhātu is realized.
The term *hrī* (紇利) is also said to mean "shame" (*lajjā*).
If one possesses both shame and dread of blame, one will not commit any unwholesome deeds;
thus, one is endowed with all untainted wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*).
Therefore, the Lotus Family is also called the Dharma Family.
Through the empowerment of these syllables,
[one is established] in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
The water birds and the forest trees all proclaim the sound of the Dharma,
as described in detail in the extensive sūtras.
If a person upholds this single-syllable mantra...
It can eliminate all calamities and diseases;
after the end of one's life, one shall be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, attaining the highest grade of the highest birth.
This single chapter applies universally to practitioners of the heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara who cultivate visualization.
It can also assist other practitioners of yoga belonging to different schools.
The above concludes the chapter on the "Prajñāpāramitā-naya" of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bhagavān, having explained as before, [remained silent].
The Tathāgata Sovereign of All Three Realms is Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha;
he is a manifestation of Ratnasaṃbhava.
This is the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja.
Furthermore, it is said that this is the bodhisattva’s mode of practice.
"The treasury of the wisdom of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas" is an alternative name for the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
"The Principle of Prajñā" has been explained as previously stated.
That is to say, by means of the gift of empowerment, one is able to attain the rank of Dharma King over the three realms;
this is the samādhi practice of the Bodhisattva Vajraratna.
That is to say, by means of the gift of meaningful benefit, all wishes and intentions are fulfilled.
This is the samādhi of the Bodhisattva Vajraprabha,
which is called "attaining the perfection of all dharmas through the gift of Dharma.
This is the practice of the samādhi of the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja.
That which is called "the bestowing of growth" results in the attainment of all peace and happiness of body, speech, and mind;
this is the samādhi practice of the Bodhisattva Vajrahasa.
Regarding the bestowing of empowerment, for whichever type of yogin it may be, one should visualize oneself as the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
He confers the consecration of the vajra-jewel upon all Tathāgatas;
as a bestower of benefit,
he provides śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas with all necessary requisites for their sustenance.
As for the gift of Dharma,
it consists of teaching the Dharma to the eight classes of beings, such as devas and nāgas, without manifesting a physical form.
The "proliferating giver" is one who bestows gifts upon the class of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
This is because the practitioner cultivates the practice of the *samādhi* of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
One should establish the fundamental maṇḍala of the Bodhisattva.
In the center of the maṇḍala, one should paint the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha in his original form;
in front of him, one should paint a vajra-jewel.
To the right, paint Vajraprabha;
to the left, paint Vajraketu;
and behind, paint Vajrahāsa.
At each of the four corners of both the inner and outer courtyards,
arrange the four inner and outer offerings according to their original forms.
Place a vajra at the eastern gate,
a jewel at the southern gate,
and a lotus at the western gate.
The Bell of the Northern Gate:
If a practitioner enters this maṇḍala,
they shall cause all the wealth, nobility, and ranks sought by others in their present life to be fully attained.
It extinguishes all karmic obstacles of poverty.
Even if one should steal property belonging to an owner,
one shall not incur the offense of taking what was not given, provided that one does not take more than one-sixth of the value.
One will swiftly attain all siddhis. Alternatively,
at times, the yogin sits within the maṇḍala and performs the yoga-visualization of the deity.
Surrounded by the assembly of noble ones,
he invokes them with the four-syllable vidyā-mantra and then recites the heart-mantra.
Through the fourfold gateways of principle,
they direct their minds throughout the entire dharma-realm,
compassionately pitying those who are impoverished, orphaned, and destitute.
They constantly practice giving with the three spheres purified and a mind free from stinginess,
always remaining in accord with the samādhi equal to space.
Before long, one attains the body of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.

Then, the Great Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, wishing to further clarify this meaning, smiled with a joyful countenance and bound a vajra-jewel garland upon his head. He then spoke the "Jewel Heart of All Empowerment Samaya," the syllable *TĀṂ*, which consists of four characters.

The fourfold gateways of practice for the principle of the *tathatā* (suchness) of many syllables signify: the meaning of the unattainability [of self] through the syllable *ra*; the meaning of being free from dust through the syllable *aḥ*; the meaning that all phenomena are originally quiescent like space through the syllable *maṃ*; and the meaning that all phenomena are without self.
Because one is constantly in accord with this heart-mantra,
body and mind are unimpeded, like empty space.
This is according to the *tathāgata-dhātu* method.
In this particular section, accomplishment is attained most swiftly;
all sought-after treasures (*nidhi*) will manifest before one.
This is because the *cintāmaṇi* jewel can fulfill all the hopes and aspirations of sentient beings. Thus concludes the *Gaganagañja-parivarta*, as previously explained by the Bhagavān.
The Tathāgata Sarvatathāgatajñānamudrā is an alternative name for Amoghasiddhi;
it is further explained as being the same as the previous interpretation.
The empowerment through the wisdom-seal (*jñāna-mudrā*) of all Tathāgatas refers to the Vajra of Body,
Speech, and Mind, which are the gateways of the three secrets.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-naya* is as explained previously.
The four seals are taught as follows:
that which holds the body-seal of all Tathāgatas becomes the body of all Tathāgatas;
this is the samādhi-body of the Bodhisattva Vajrakarma.
By virtue of attaining the empowerment of the body,
the mantra practitioner attains an unimpeded body and performs vast offerings throughout infinite worlds.
"Holding the speech-mudrā of all Tathāgatas, one then attains the dharmas of all Tathāgatas;
this is called the Bodhisattva Vajrapāla Samādhi. By means of this samādhi..."
He is able to universally protect the boundless realm of sentient beings,
constantly adorning himself with the armor of great compassion,
and has attained the indestructible diamond-like Dharma-body.
By holding the heart-seal (hṛdaya-mudrā) of all Tathāgatas, one realizes the samādhi of all Tathāgatas;
through this, the mantra-practitioner attains the Vajrayakṣa-samādhi.
He is able to exhaust the seeds of affliction consisting of the intent to kill within the ālayavijñāna;
having attained the samādhi of great skillful means and great compassion,
he manifests for the sake of subduing others in the form of the Bodhisattva Vajrayakṣa, fierce and wrathful.
One who holds the vajra-mudrā of all Tathāgatas achieves the supreme siddhi of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas;
this is because the practitioner of yoga attains the bodhisattva samādhi of Vajramuṣṭi.
One is able to accomplish the gateway of the three secrets within all mantra teachings.
Therefore, it is said in the Extensive Yoga (Vistara-yoga):
"The union of the vajras of body, speech, and mind is called the fist."
The binding of all Tathāgatas is the Vajra Fist.
Therefore, the Buddha told Vajrapāṇi: "If anyone hears this principle, receives and upholds it, recites it, and contemplates it with focused attention..."

"By holding the body mudrā, one attains all accomplishments"—this phrase appears as the first function in the Sanskrit original, while in the Chinese version it occurs in the fourth [section]. "By holding the speech mudrā, one attains mastery over all speech."
By holding the mind-seal (cittamudrā), one attains the wisdom of all wisdoms;
by holding the vajra-seal (vajramudrā), all activities are fully accomplished,
and one swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
A practitioner who wishes to accomplish the yoga of the Prajñā-naya should establish the Vajramuṣṭi maṇḍala; in its center,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Sarvatathāgatamuṣṭi.
In front, paint Vajrakarma;
on the right, paint Vajrarakṣa;
and on the left, paint Vajrayakṣa.
Next, paint the vajra-fist.
In each of the four inner and outer corners, place the four inner and four outer offerings.
At the four gates, place the four bodhisattvas.
At the eastern gate is Rājika-vajra;
at the southern gate, Vajramuṣṭi-likhita;
at the western gate, Priya-vajra.
The Vajra Pride at the Northern Gate:
At times, the yogin, dwelling within the maṇḍala,
performs the yoga of himself as the principal deity.
Visualize that all the retinues each abide in their original positions;
then, with the four-syllable vidyā-mantra, invoke all the assembly of noble ones,
reciting the one-syllable mantra.
Then, one recites the four kinds of Vajramuṣṭi Prajñāpāramitā-naya,
applying the mudrās and directing the mind through each gateway of the nayas;
its extent is equal to the Dharma-realm, revolving again and again.
All samādhis manifest before one; the syllable *akṣara* (the "evil" letter) signifies the meaning of nirvāṇa.
The four kinds of nirvāṇa are subsumed within this single syllable.
As for these four kinds, they are as explained previously.

Then, the Bhagavān, desiring to clarify this meaning, smiled with a joyful countenance, assumed the Great Samaya Seal of the Vajra Fist, and spoke this Heart Mantra of the Self-Reality of All Solid Vajra-Seal Siddhis and Samayas.

The above meanings of the phrases express the majestic demeanor of the Great Wisdom Seal (Mahājñānamudrā) of the original Bodhisattva, while also praising the efficacy of the Secret Speech (Vāgguhya).
This concludes the ritual manual for the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi; the above is the chapter on the Vajramuṣṭi-principle from the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.
At that time, the Bhagavān Sarvanirjalpa Tathāgata—
another name for the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī—
further expounded the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya* of the Turning Wheel of Syllables.
The "turning of the wheel of syllables" refers to the samādhi of the five-syllable wheel;
that is to say, because all phenomena correspond with emptiness and the absence of intrinsic nature.
This is the *vajratīkṣṇa-bodhisattva-samādhi* within the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala.
It is so called because all phenomena are signless and correspond to the nature of signlessness.
"This is the *vajratīkṣṇa-samādhi* of Trailokyavijaya-maṇḍala;
'because all phenomena are associated with wishlessness and wishlessness' refers to the *padmatīkṣṇa-bodhisattva-samādhi* within the Sarvārthasiddhi-maṇḍala."
Regarding "the radiance of all phenomena through the purification of the Prajñāpāramitā":
this refers to the *ratnaprabhāsa-samādhi* of the Bodhisattva Ratnolkā within the Maṇḍala of the Accomplishment of All Aims (*Sarvārthasiddhi*).
The practitioner of yoga who accomplishes the perfection of wisdom should establish a maṇḍala.
As for the maṇḍala:
Arrange the forms of eight maṇḍalas.
In the center, paint the form of the youth Mañjuśrī;
in the four directions, place the four Buddhas.
With the sword of space-like wisdom,
bind each of the four Buddhas' arms;
in the four corners, place the seals of the four kinds of Prajñāpāramitā.
At the four outer corners, place the four outer offerings;
at the four gates, place the four types of mudrās.
At the eastern gate, draw a sword.
On the south gate, paint Śakti;
on the west gate, a bowl;
on the north gate, Brahmakavaca.
At times, the yoga practitioner sits within the maṇḍala,
performs the yoga of the deity,
and directs the mind to arrange the assembly of noble beings.
Invoke with the four-syllable vidyā-mantra;
when reciting the one-syllable vidyā-mantra,
one recites the fourfold Prajñāpāramitā-naya.
It is associated with the mind;
it pervades the entire dharma-realm, circling and beginning again,
for as long as one month, six months, or even a year.
Before long, you shall attain unimpeded eloquence,
realize immeasurable gateways of samādhi,
and have Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva appear before you.

Then, the youthful Mañjuśrī, wishing to further clarify this meaning, smiled with a joyful countenance and, brandishing his own sword, struck all the Tathāgatas who had previously spoken of this most supreme heart of the Prajñāpāramitā.
All sentient beings, in the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra,
have accumulated immeasurable false afflictions together with the four types of consciousness.
Thus one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
While in the stage of an ordinary person, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*);
upon entering the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*) up to the stage of a Tathāgata, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
By means of the four wisdoms of enlightenment,
one counteracts the four kinds of deluded consciousness;
once deluded consciousness is eliminated, the dharma-wisdom is brought to maturity.
If one falsely adheres to phenomena,
it constitutes the affliction of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*);
therefore, a Bodhisattva who has increased wisdom employs the fourfold sword of Mañjuśrī’s Prajñāpāramitā.
By severing the four kinds of cognitive faculties that constitute the obstacles of subject and object,
one attains Buddhahood; for this reason,
Mañjuśrī manifested the act of hacking off the arms of the four Buddhas.
The syllable AṂ is the supreme mind of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The syllable AṂ signifies awakening.
There are four kinds of awakening.
That is to say: the awakening of the śrāvakas,
the awakening of the pratyekabuddhas,
and the awakening of the bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgata has awakened to this.
Although the names and phrases used for awakening are the same,
there are differences in their depth and significance.
The accumulations for one’s own benefit and the benefit of others differ in their small and great degrees;
by means of the four types of awakening,
all mundane, supramundane, and supreme supramundane [teachings] are comprehensively subsumed.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva has attained mastery over the Dharma;
thus he is called the Son of the Dharma King. The above concludes the "Chapter on the Rational System of Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Bhagavān, the Tathāgata of All Tathāgatas, entered the Great Wheel Tathāgata.
This is another name for a bodhisattva who has just resolved their mind [on enlightenment].
Furthermore, it explains the entrance into the principle of the Great Wheel Prajñā.
As for the "Great Wheel":
This is the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu.
It is said that entering the equality of the vajra is to enter the Dharma-wheel of all Tathāgatas;
this is by means of the samādhi of the Vajracakra of the Prajñāpāramitā-naya.
Thus, one enters the Vajradhātu.
This has already been explained within the *Sixfold Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu* (Vajradhātu-ṣaṭprakāra-maṇḍala-nirdeśa).
As for "entering the equality of meaning, one enters the wheel of the Great Bodhisattvas":
By reciting this *prajñāpāramitā*-naya of the Wrathful Wheel (*krodhacakra*),
one accomplishes entry into Trailokyavijaya;
this has already been explained previously among the ten types of mandalas belonging to Trailokyavijaya within the "Tenfold Pointers" (*daśavidha-aṅgulī-nirdeśa*).
To enter the equality of all phenomena is to enter the sublime wheel of Dharma;
by invoking this samādhi of the Lotus Wheel of the Principle of Prajñā,
one achieves entry into universal subduing.
This belongs to the Universal Subjugation [mandala].
Regarding the six types of maṇḍalas, they are formed by offering the four mudrās of the subtle dharmas of the Great Secret;
thus, the six types of altars are established. These six types have already been explained in detail in the aforementioned "Pointing to the Goal" (Zhigui).
Entering into the equality of all actions is to enter the wheel of all ritual activities (*karmakriyā*).
By means of this samādhi of the *karmamudrā* of the principle of Prajñāpāramitā,
one accomplishes entry into the fulfillment of all purposes.
This pertains to the sixfold maṇḍala of Sarvārthasiddhi.
In order to further clarify this meaning, the Great Bodhisattva Sadyo-mānasī-cakra-pravartana, with a joyful smile, turned the vajra-wheel and spoke the heart-mantra of all vajra-samayas.
As explained in the preceding section on the meaning of the phrases:
the form of the Great Wisdom Seal (*mahājñānamudrā*) of the Bodhisattva Vajracakra is the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is the Vajrasamaya Heart.
The syllable HŪṂ possesses the meaning of the four wheels.
If one practices the samādhi of the Bodhisattva Vajracakra,
one should construct a maṇḍala.
Draw the shape of an eight-spoked wheel.
In the center of the hub of the wheel,
draw the Bodhisattva Vajracakra.
Within the eight spokes,
paint the eight great bodhisattvas,
arranged as previously described.
In the four corners outside the eight wheels,
paint the four Pāramitā Bodhisattvas; in the four corners of the inner courtyard, [paint the same].
Place the four inner offerings within;
place the four outer offerings at the four corners outside.
Within the inner enclosure, four gates are established, each housing a bodhisattva:
at the eastern gate is Vajrasattva Bodhisattva;
at the southern gate is Trailokyavijaya-vajra.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is at the western gate;
Ākāśagarbha is at the northern gate.
The practitioner of yoga violates the samaya.
Alternatively, if an ācārya has lost his position as a teacher through unrighteous conduct,
by establishing this maṇḍala-cakra,
he shall restore his original status as an ācārya.
By practicing all samādhis and mantras,
one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
If one leads a disciple [into the mandala],...
If one enters by means of oneself,
then one accomplishes entry into all mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas;
alternatively, at times the yoga-ācārya sits within the maṇḍala himself.
Directing the mind, arrange the various assemblies of holy ones.
To invite these assemblies with the four-syllable vidyā-mantra, recite the one-syllable mantra.
Next, recite the *Caturvidha-cakra-prajñāpāramitā-naya*.

Directing the mind so that it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, before long one shall attain the status of a Wheel-Turning Dharma King like Vairocana Buddha. [The above is from the "Chapter on the Principles for Bodhisattvas Who Have Just Awakened the Resolve."]
At that time, the Bhagavān, the Tathāgata of the Vast Ritual of the Treasury of Various Offerings of All Tathāgatas,
is another name for the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
Furthermore, it is taught that the supreme source of all offerings is the principle of prajñā, namely: "To generate the bodhicitta is itself the vast offering to all Tathāgatas."
This is the meaning of the bodhicitta of the Vajra-lalita Bodhisattva’s samādhi.
All Tathāgatas take bodhicitta as the dominant condition for attaining buddhahood.
To delight in the garden of the Dharma of bodhicitta and to find joy in the perfection of wisdom,
thereby rescuing all sentient beings— this constitutes a vast offering to all the Tathāgatas.
This is the samādhi of the Bodhisattva Vajramālā.
Through pure faith, one enters the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma and obtains the wish-fulfilling garland of the seven jewels.
To deliver all sentient beings,
to fulfill all their aspirations and wishes,
and to cause all sentient beings to receive the various categories of precepts.
Adorning oneself in this way and upholding the sublime scriptures constitutes a vast offering to all Tathāgatas;
this is the Vajragīti Bodhisattva Samādhi.
By means of this samādhi,

one will be able to engage in questions and answers regarding all the profound Prajñāpāramitā of the Mahāyāna within the assemblies of the Buddhas. Furthermore, to uphold, recite, read, copy, teach others to copy, contemplate, and cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā, and to offer various kinds of worship to it, constitutes a vast offering to all the Tathāgatas.
This is the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Vajra Dance Offering.
Through great diligence and the liberating wisdom of Vajraviśvakarman,
one travels throughout infinite worlds.
Before all the Buddhas, he made vast offerings and requested them to preach all the Buddha-dharmas, such as the Prajñāpāramitā and other sūtras,
by means of the ten dharma-practices.
Suddenly accumulating the two kinds of provisions— merit and wisdom—
he attains the three bodies.
This Bodhisattva presides over all gateways of offering.
There are many types of offering gates.
According to the Susiddhi teachings,
there are five kinds of offerings.
Furthermore, there are twenty kinds of offerings.
Within the Yoga teachings, there are four kinds of offerings, namely: the offering of the bodhicitta.
The offering of provisions,
the offering of the Dharma,
and the offering of ritual action.
These are the four types of gates of reasoning as previously described.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of secret offerings,
and there are also eight kinds of offerings.
Furthermore, there are sixteen kinds of great offerings,
as well as seventeen, six, or even all manner of miscellaneous offerings;
all of these are fully subsumed within the *Vajrapāṇi-ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-pūjā-vidhi*.
If a practitioner desires to achieve the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
they should establish a maṇḍala and paint the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja in its center.
The right hand holds a karma-vajra;
the left hand forms a vajra-fist and rests upon the left hip.
Seated in the half-lotus posture upon a moon disc,
surrounded by the eight great bodhisattvas,
with the eight offerings placed in the four inner and outer corners.
The four gates should be furnished with four kinds of jewels:
silver at the eastern gate and gold at the southern gate.
A maṇi jewel is placed at the western gate,
and pearls are placed at the northern gate.
At times, the practitioner sits within the maṇḍala.
Perform the yoga visualization of oneself as the principal deity,
surrounded by the assembly of noble beings,
and invoke them with the four-syllable mantra.
While holding the single-syllable mantra,
one recites the fourfold *prajñāpāramitā-naya*,
directing the mind throughout the entire dharma-realm, beginning again from where it ended.
Until samādhi manifests before him,
he should either enter this maṇḍala himself or cause others to enter it, and thereafter uphold the single-syllable mantra,
perhaps adding various offering implements such as incense and flowers.
If one can direct the mind to make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
then the offering implements will pervade the entire Dharma-realm,
and before each and every Buddha and Bodhisattva, a vast and magnificent offering will be accomplished.
Then, the Great Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, wishing to further clarify and illuminate this meaning, smiled with a joyful countenance and spoke these words:
"The All-Vajra Heart of the Non-in Vain Samaya of All Activities."
As previously explained,
the mind-mantra is the syllable Oṃ. The syllable Oṃ signifies the three bodies (trikāya).
It is also called the meaning of the invisible crown of the head;
it is also called the meaning of primordial non-arising;
and it is also the meaning of the merit of the Tathāgata’s ūrṇā-kośa (hair-treasure). This concludes the "Chapter on the Principles of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva."
The term "Bhagavān" is as explained previously.
"The Tathāgata who holds the Wisdom Fist (Jñānamuṣṭi) capable of subduing" is an alternative name for the Bodhisattva Sarvamārapramardin.
Alternatively, it is called the "Prajñāpāramitā Principle of the Treasury of Wisdom for Subduing All.
That which is termed "the equality of wrath due to the equality of all sentient beings" is the Vajra Trailokyavijaya Samādhi.
By means of this samādhi, he subdues the Māra-king Vaśavartin of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin realm,
leading those to be converted into the path of the Buddha.
Because all sentient beings are thus subdued, wrath itself is subdued.
This is the Jewel-Vajra Wrathful Samādhi within the Jewel Family.
By means of this concentration, one is able to subdue Maheśvara and cause him to be transformed and enter the Buddha-way.
"Because the dharmatā of all sentient beings is the dharmatā of wrath"—
this is the samādhi of Hayagrīva, the Wrathful Avalokiteśvara, within the Lotus Family.
By means of this samādhi, he subdued Brahmā and caused him to enter the Buddha-way through transformation.
Because all sentient beings possess the nature of vajra, they possess the nature of wrathful vajra.
This is the karma-samādhi within the Karma-varga.
By means of this samādhi, Nārāyaṇa was subdued,
converted, and led to enter the Buddha-way.
Why is it that the taming of all sentient beings is itself enlightenment?
It is because this was originally the Bodhisattva Maitreya;
by means of this bodhisattva entering the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
Out of deep compassion for the gods who are difficult to discipline,
he manifests a fierce exterior to bring them to transformation and lead them into Bodhi.

Then, the Great Bodhisattva Sarvamārapramardin, wishing to further clarify this meaning, smiled with a joyful countenance; assuming the form of a Vajrayakṣa and brandishing vajra-fangs, he struck terror into all the Tathāgatas.
All the various devas of the non-Buddhists are fully endowed with the Tathāgatagarbha;
they are future Buddhas.
Because it causes them to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox,
it is called "Terrifying All Tathāgatas.
A Tathāgata is one who has abandoned the five fears and attained the four fearlessnesses.
There is nothing that can cause fear.
What you currently fear does not reside in the Tathāgata of the fruition stage,
but rather in the causal stage.
Regarding the explanation of the heart-mantra of the Great Laughing Vajra-Wrath:
